title: Nth Fibonacci Number
directAnswer: Iterate with two variables `a = 0`, `b = 1`, updating `(a, b) → (b, a + b)` n times. O(n) time, O(1) space — far better than naive recursion's O(2ⁿ).

remember.takeaway: When state depends on the last k values, keep k variables, not an array.
remember.formula: a,b = 0,1;  repeat n times: a,b = b, a+b;  return a
whenToUse: State depends on the last k values
antiSignals: Need many arbitrary indices fast — consider matrix power / closed form

problemStatement: Given `n` (0-indexed), return the Nth Fibonacci number, where `F(0) = 0`, `F(1) = 1`, and `F(k) = F(k-1) + F(k-2)`.
understanding: Carry just the last two values and roll them forward n times — no array or recursion needed.

approaches.name: Iterative two-variable roll
approaches.whenToMention: This is the standard, expected solution — lead with it.
approaches.explanation:
Each Fibonacci number is the sum of the previous two, so you only ever need to remember the last two values. Roll a pair `(a, b)` forward n times: `(a, b) → (b, a + b)`. O(n) time, O(1) space.

**Why not plain recursion.** The naive `fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2)` recomputes the same subproblems exponentially — fib(50) makes ~2.5 billion calls. The iterative roll computes each value once. Naming that O(2ⁿ) blow-up and replacing it with O(n) is the entire interview signal.

**Why two variables suffice.** The recurrence has 'order 2' — the next value depends only on the two before it. Whenever state depends on the last k values, you keep k variables, not the whole history. This is the seed of space-optimised dynamic programming.

**Overflow.** Fibonacci grows ~1.618ⁿ, so F(91) overflows 64-bit long. With `long`, n ≤ 90 is the safe range — beyond that you'd need BigInteger.
hints: Each value needs only the previous two. Do you really need an array?
Roll two variables forward: (a, b) becomes (b, a + b).
Avoid naive recursion — it's exponential. Watch overflow past F(90).
approaches.insight: Naming the recursion's O(2ⁿ) cost and then giving the O(n) loop is the standout move on this classic.
approaches.complexityReasoning: one addition per step for n steps, holding just two values.

dryRun.intro: Slide the two-value window forward n times.

edgeCases.behavior: Loop runs zero times; returns a = 0 = F(0).
Largest F that fits in long; F(91) overflows.

pitfalls: Using naive recursion and timing out at O(2ⁿ).
Off-by-one in the loop bound or returning b instead of a.

commonMistakes: Using naive recursion (O(2ⁿ)) and timing out.

patternNote: A core fresher pattern: Rolling two variables. Master it on small inputs and it transfers to harder problems.

clarifyingQuestions.answer: I'll assume F(0)=0, F(1)=1 — confirm the indexing matters for the answer.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How large is n?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up to ~90 for long; bigger needs BigInteger.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Naive exponential recursion
commonMistakesDetailed.why: fib(n-1)+fib(n-2) recomputes overlapping subproblems, making ~2ⁿ calls; fib(50) is already billions.
